passage: Monday: The headmistress read out the essay prize winner: Kamal. Jeevan had wanted it so badly he'd rewritten his three times. He clapped with everyone, face stiff, and said, “Well done,” without looking at Kamal. At home he threw his bag on the bed. “I'm so jealous I could scream,” he told Amma. She said, “That's allowed. Say it here. You don't have to say it there.” Wednesday: Jeevan found Kamal by the water cooler. “Your ending was really good. The bit about the kite.” Kamal grinned. “Yours was close. Sir said so.” Friday: Jeevan asked Kamal how he'd thought of the kite. They talked through the whole lunch break.

qa.q: How many times had Jeevan rewritten his essay?
qa.a: Jeevan had rewritten it three times.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling as he clapped with a stiff face?
qa.a: Jeevan felt jealous and disappointed, having wanted the prize badly, but he managed to clap anyway.

qa.q: How did Amma help Jeevan handle his envy?
qa.a: She said the feeling was allowed and could be named privately at home, without having to show it to Kamal.

qa.q: How did Kamal respond to Jeevan's compliment on Wednesday?
qa.a: Kamal grinned and told Jeevan his essay had been close, which made them friends rather than rivals.

grounding: Shows a child managing envy enough to congratulate a winning friend, while naming the feeling privately at home.

passage: Jahnavi, you clapped for your friend today with a face like a closed door. Let your Sarita Mausi tell you a secret. When I was eleven, my best friend Rupa got the solo in the school choir. I had practised that song for weeks. When they announced her name, I clapped louder than anyone and smiled so hard my cheeks hurt. That night I had a stomach ache and couldn't say why. My mother sat on my bed and asked, “Are you sad about the solo?” I burst into tears. “I'm happy for Rupa. And I'm jealous. Both.” She said, “Both is honest.” The next day, clapping for Rupa felt real.

qa.q: What did Rupa get in the school choir?
qa.a: Rupa got the solo.

qa.q: What was young Sarita feeling as she clapped louder than anyone?
qa.a: She felt jealous and disappointed but hid it behind a big smile, which later came out as a stomach ache and tears.

qa.q: What choice did Sarita's mother make, and why did it help?
qa.a: She asked gently if Sarita was sad about the solo, which let her name both happiness and jealousy, making the next day's clapping real.

qa.q: How might Rupa have experienced Sarita's clapping?
qa.a: Rupa probably saw only a happy friend clapping loudly, not knowing about the hidden jealousy.

grounding: Shows a child celebrating a friend's success while hiding envy, and naming the feeling privately proving healthier than pretending.

passage: The chess final had ended in twenty minutes, and now the photographer was rushing everyone onto the stage. As runner-up, Usha had to stand beside Kamal while he held up the trophy she'd wanted all year. Her throat felt tight. There was no time to go off and be sad; the camera was already flashing. She turned, held out her hand and said, “Well played. Your knight move was brilliant.” Kamal shook it, surprised and pleased. After the photos, Usha found her coach in the corridor. “I'm really disappointed,” she said, and her voice wobbled. “Good,” said the coach. “Say it to me. And you were a proper sport up there.”

qa.q: How long did the chess final take?
qa.a: The chess final ended in twenty minutes.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling as she stood beside Kamal on stage?
qa.a: Usha felt disappointed and tight-throated, having wanted the trophy all year.

qa.q: How did Usha manage both celebrating Kamal and her own feelings?
qa.a: She congratulated him sincerely on stage, then told her coach privately that she was really disappointed.

qa.q: How did Kamal react to Usha's handshake?
qa.a: Kamal was surprised and pleased by her sincere compliment.

grounding: Shows a child congratulating a rival who won while disappointed, then naming the feeling privately to a trusted adult.

passage: When Thabo went home with Bilal after school in Durban, he noticed something new. At the door, Bilal said, “Salaam, Dadi-ji,” to his grandmother and bent his head as she touched it. To the lady from next door he said, “Hello, Aunty,” though she wasn't his aunt. Thabo whispered, “Is everyone your aunty?” Bilal grinned. “Older ladies, yes. It's respect.” Thabo thought about his own gran in Umlazi, and how he called older women “Mama” even if they were strangers. “We do that too. Just a different word.” When Dadi-ji brought samosas, Thabo said, “Thank you, Dadi-ji,” carefully. She laughed and gave him two.

qa.q: What did Thabo call older women at home?
qa.a: Thabo called older women “Mama”, even if they were strangers.

qa.q: What was Thabo feeling when Dadi-ji laughed and gave him two samosas?
qa.a: Thabo probably felt pleased and welcomed after carefully using the respectful name.

qa.q: How did Bilal explain the word Aunty?
qa.a: He explained that calling older ladies Aunty is a way of showing respect, not about being related.

qa.q: How might Dadi-ji have felt when Thabo used her respectful name?
qa.a: She probably felt touched and amused, and showed it by laughing and giving him an extra samosa.

grounding: Shows a child greeting elders with respectful address like ji and aunty, and how such forms vary between families and cultures.

passage: When Lakshmi Ma'am, who had taught at the school for thirty years, visited on Founders' Day, the children of Class 6 lined up in the corridor to greet her. Tanuja bent and touched her feet, the way she did with her own grandmother. Lakshmi Ma'am rested a hand on her head. “Jeete raho.” Next came Arif, who said “Adaab, Ma'am,” with his hand raised to his forehead, and Grace, who said “Good morning, Ma'am,” and smiled. Tanuja wondered if the others were being less respectful. Afterwards she asked Lakshmi Ma'am. “Every one of those greetings was respect,” the old teacher said. “Each family teaches its own way.”

qa.q: How long had Lakshmi Ma'am taught at the school?
qa.a: She had taught at the school for thirty years.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling when she saw the other greetings?
qa.a: Tanuja felt unsure, wondering whether the other children's greetings were less respectful than touching feet.

qa.q: What did Tanuja do to settle her doubt?
qa.a: She asked Lakshmi Ma'am directly, who explained that every greeting was respect taught in each family's own way.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi Ma'am see the different greetings?
qa.a: She saw each greeting, touching feet, adaab and good morning, as equally respectful.

grounding: Shows children showing respect to an elder by touching feet, adaab or a greeting, with the form varying by family and faith.

passage: I'm Sangeeta, from the flat above, and I watched Kiran settle in after the family moved back from Chicago. The first week, Kiran waved from the stairs and called, “Hi, Sangeeta!” My husband raised his eyebrows. I didn't mind, but Kiran's grandmother did. I heard her through the window that evening: “Aunty, beta. Or Sangeeta-ji. That's how we show respect here.” The next morning Kiran stood at my door with the newspaper I'd dropped. “Good morning, Sangeeta Aunty.” A small pause. “Is that right?” I said it was perfect. I don't know if Kiran liked the change, but the smile looked proud.

qa.q: Where did Kiran's family move back from?
qa.a: They moved back from Chicago.

qa.q: What might Kiran have been feeling when asking “Is that right?”
qa.a: Kiran probably felt a little unsure but eager to get the new, respectful form of address right, and then proud.

qa.q: How did Kiran's grandmother teach the custom?
qa.a: She explained calmly that saying Aunty or Sangeeta-ji is how respect is shown there.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta feel about being called by her first name?
qa.a: Sangeeta didn't mind, though she noticed her husband and Kiran's grandmother saw it differently.

grounding: Shows a child learning respectful address such as ji and aunty for elders, a form that varies by family and region.

passage: The canteen was roaring, the bell was about to go, and Anirban had exactly one minute to find Aadhya. He'd been off sick all week, and she had copied her science notes for him, neat, with diagrams in two colours. He spotted her in the queue and pushed through. “Aadhya! Your notes. Thank you. The diagram of the heart was better than the textbook's.” Aadhya blinked. “You actually read them?” “Twice. I'd have failed the test without them.” She smiled, pleased and a bit pink. The bell rang. “Next time you're sick,” she called after him, “I'll do the maths too!”

qa.q: How long had Anirban been off sick?
qa.a: Anirban had been off sick all week.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling when Anirban thanked her?
qa.a: Aadhya felt surprised and pleased, a bit pink, that he had really read and valued her notes.

qa.q: Why did Anirban's thanks come across as sincere?
qa.a: He named something specific, the heart diagram, and said how the notes had helped him, even in a rush.

qa.q: What would change if Anirban had only mumbled “thanks” in passing?
qa.a: Aadhya might have felt her careful work went unnoticed and been less keen to help next time.

grounding: Shows a child thanking a classmate for help with a specific, sincere compliment.

passage: In their Pune classroom, Tarun leaned over Bhavna's desk. “Wow, your drawing is amazing. You're the best artist in the class.” Bhavna felt her cheeks warm. Then he added, “Can I borrow your gold pen?” She lent it. The next day: “Your handwriting is so neat.” Then: “Can I copy your homework?” Bhavna frowned. Every compliment came with a request. On Friday, her friend Sana said, “I love how you did the sky,” and then just went back to her own work. That one felt different. Bhavna kept it in her head all day. When Tarun started his next compliment, she said, “Thanks. What do you need?” He laughed, caught out.

qa.q: What did Tarun ask to borrow after the first compliment?
qa.a: Tarun asked to borrow her gold pen.

qa.q: What was Bhavna feeling when she noticed every compliment came with a request?
qa.a: Bhavna felt uneasy and a bit let down, sensing Tarun's praise was a way to get favours.

qa.q: How did Bhavna respond to Tarun's next compliment, and why was it fair?
qa.a: She thanked him and asked what he needed, calmly naming the pattern without being rude.

qa.q: What made Sana's compliment feel different?
qa.a: Sana praised something specific and asked for nothing in return, so it felt sincere.

grounding: Shows compliments that are sincere next to compliments used to gain favour, and how context shapes how they are heard.

passage: “That goal!” Thomas jogged over, panting. “The way you curled it round the defender. How did you even do that?” Nazia grinned. “You passed it to me perfectly, that's how. I just had to hit it.” “No, the curl was all you.” “Okay, the curl was me. But thanks for the pass. And for staying back to practise with me on Tuesday.” Thomas shrugged, trying not to look pleased. “You'd have got it anyway.” “Maybe in a year.” Their coach, collecting cones, looked over. “Listen to you two. That's what a team sounds like.” Thomas held up a hand, and Nazia high-fived it.

qa.q: When did Thomas stay back to practise with Nazia?
qa.a: Thomas stayed back to practise with Nazia on Tuesday.

qa.q: What was Thomas feeling when shrugging off the thanks?
qa.a: Thomas felt pleased by the thanks but a bit shy about showing it.

qa.q: What made the compliments between Thomas and Nazia sincere?
qa.a: Each named something specific, the curl and the pass, and the praise went both ways without anyone asking for anything.

qa.q: How did the coach see the exchange?
qa.a: The coach saw it as the sound of a good team, with each player crediting the other.

grounding: Shows children complimenting a goal and thanking each other for help, with reciprocity making the praise feel sincere.

passage: I'm Vikas. When the list for the inter-school quiz went up, Hira's name wasn't on it. She walked off to the bench by the gate. Nazia went after her. “Oh, poor you,” I heard her say. “That's so sad. You must feel terrible.” Hira stiffened. “I don't feel terrible. I'm angry. Sir picked his favourites.” Nazia stopped. I don't know what went through her head, but her voice changed. “Sorry. I guessed wrong. Do you want company, or do you want to be alone for a bit?” Hira kicked at the gravel. “Company. But don't say poor me.” Nazia sat down next to her, and they didn't say anything for a while.

qa.q: Where did Hira go after seeing the list?
qa.a: Hira walked off to the bench by the gate.

qa.q: What was Hira feeling when she stiffened at “poor you”?
qa.a: Hira felt angry, not sad, and the pity made her feel more annoyed.

qa.q: What did Nazia change that helped?
qa.a: She admitted she guessed wrong and asked whether Hira wanted company or space, instead of telling her how she felt.

qa.q: How did Vikas notice the change in Nazia?
qa.a: Vikas heard Nazia's voice change after Hira's reply, though Vikas couldn't know exactly what Nazia was thinking.

grounding: Shows a child moving from feeling sorry for a friend to asking do you want company, after guessing the friend's feeling wrongly.

passage: Monday: Baljeet's new cycle was stolen from outside the library. Disha rushed over. “Oh no, I'm so sorry for you! My cousin's got stolen too, and he cried for days, and…” Baljeet stared at the empty stand and said nothing. Disha kept talking. He walked off alone. Tuesday: Disha thought about it all night. She'd felt sorry for him, but she hadn't asked what he felt. At break she found him. “I talked too much yesterday. Do you want company walking home, now you're on foot?” Baljeet nodded. Wednesday: On the long walk, Baljeet finally said, “I saved for two years for that cycle.” Disha just listened. This time she didn't guess.

qa.q: Where was Baljeet's cycle stolen from?
qa.a: It was stolen from outside the library.

qa.q: What was Baljeet feeling as he stared at the empty stand?
qa.a: Baljeet was shocked and upset, too stunned to talk about the cycle he had saved for.

qa.q: What did Disha change on Tuesday, and why did it help?
qa.a: She admitted talking too much and simply offered company on the walk home, which let Baljeet share his feelings when ready.

qa.q: What was Monday like for Baljeet with Disha talking?
qa.a: Baljeet likely felt unheard, as Disha's stories about her cousin filled the space where his own feelings should have been.

grounding: Shows a child learning the difference between feeling sorry for a friend and feeling with him, and asking do you want company.

passage: Gopika, you asked how to help your friend whose house flooded. Let your Vishal Nana tell you what I got wrong once. When I was ten, the river rose and my friend Harihar's hut was washed out. The next day at school, I rushed up and said, “Poor Harihar! You must be so sad! You've lost everything!” He went red and turned away. I didn't understand. Our teacher took me aside. “You told him how he feels. Ask him instead.” So at lunch I asked, “Do you want me to sit with you, or leave you be?” Harihar said, very quietly, “Sit.” We didn't talk. After a while he said, “We saved the goat.” And he smiled.

qa.q: What did Harihar's family save?
qa.a: They saved the goat.

qa.q: What was Harihar feeling when he went red and turned away?
qa.a: Harihar felt embarrassed and hurt at being pitied loudly, and perhaps wasn't ready to hear his loss described.

qa.q: What choice did young Vishal make after the teacher's advice, and why did it work?
qa.a: He asked whether Harihar wanted company or to be left alone, then sat quietly, which let Harihar share in his own time.

qa.q: What did the teacher notice about Vishal's first attempt?
qa.a: The teacher noticed Vishal had told Harihar how he felt instead of asking.

grounding: Shows a child learning that guessing a friend's feelings can be wrong, and that asking do you want company is wiser.

subtype: Encouraging a friend before a challenge [Expressing]
passage: “I can't do it, Tanvir. My legs feel like noodles.” Sabina stood at the edge of the pool, shivering. “You're nervous. That's normal. I'm always nervous before a race.” “You are?” “Every time. My stomach does flips.” Sabina almost smiled. “So what do you do?” “I look at the far wall and only think about the first three strokes. Not the whole race. Just three.” “Three strokes.” “And you've swum this length a hundred times in practice. You can do it.” The whistle blew. Sabina looked at the far wall. One, two, three. Then she didn't stop until she touched it.

qa.q: What does Tanvir look at before a race?
qa.a: Tanvir looks at the far wall.

qa.q: What was Sabina feeling at the edge of the pool?
qa.a: Sabina felt nervous and shaky, her legs like noodles.

qa.q: Why did Tanvir's encouragement help more than just “You can do it”?
qa.a: He accepted her nervousness, shared his own and gave a concrete tip: focus on the first three strokes.

qa.q: What would change if Tanvir had said “Don't be silly, you're not nervous”?
qa.a: Sabina might have felt unheard and more anxious, with no plan to calm herself.

grounding: Shows a child encouraging a friend before a race without denying her nerves, and pairing belief with a concrete suggestion.

subtype: Encouraging a friend before a challenge [Expressing]
passage: I'm Zainab. Last year, before the maths olympiad, my friend Lokesh sat on the school steps looking grey. I said, “Don't worry! You'll be fine! You're a genius!” He looked even greyer. “You don't know that.” I felt useless. Then I remembered what my sister did for me before my dance exam: she didn't say I'd be fine; she said, “Your hands are cold. Warm them, then do the first move slowly.” So I tried again. “You're nervous, and that makes sense. Want to go over the three formulas you always forget, just once?” We did. His colour came back a bit. He came third. I learned that encouraging needs a plan, not just cheering.

qa.q: Where did Lokesh finish in the olympiad?
qa.a: Lokesh came third.

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling on the school steps?
qa.a: Lokesh was nervous and anxious before the olympiad, looking grey.

qa.q: What did Zainab change the second time, and why did it work?
qa.a: Zainab accepted his nerves and offered a concrete step, going over the three formulas he always forgets.

qa.q: Why didn't “You're a genius” help Lokesh?
qa.a: It brushed past his nerves and promised something Zainab couldn't know, so it added pressure.

grounding: Shows a child learning that encouragement before a test works best with a concrete suggestion and without denying nervousness.

subtype: Encouraging a friend before a challenge [Expressing]
passage: Coach's note, Saturday. Gopika, under-eleven hockey. Before the penalty shoot-out, our goalkeeper, Nisha, was pale and shaking. I was about to go over when I saw Jeevan get there first. I heard him say, “It's okay to be scared. I would be.” Then: “Watch their stick, not their eyes. You saved three like that on Thursday.” Nisha nodded, and her shoulders came down. She saved two out of five. We still lost, but she walked off the pitch with her head up. I told Jeevan afterwards that what he did was real encouragement: he didn't pretend she wasn't scared, and he gave her something to do. I'd like him to help me coach the younger ones.

qa.q: How many penalties did Nisha save?
qa.a: Nisha saved two out of five.

qa.q: What was Nisha feeling before the shoot-out?
qa.a: Nisha was scared and anxious, pale and shaking.

qa.q: What made Jeevan's encouragement effective?
qa.a: He accepted that she was scared and gave a concrete tip, to watch the stick, reminding her of the three she saved on Thursday.

qa.q: How did Gopika see what Jeevan did?
qa.a: Gopika saw it as real encouragement and wanted him to help coach the younger players.

grounding: Shows a child encouraging a teammate before a challenge by accepting her fear and giving a concrete suggestion.

passage: “Irawati. I have to tell you something.” Shalini held out her hands. In them were the two halves of Irawati's clay elephant. “I knocked it off the shelf with my bag. It was my fault. I'm really sorry.” Irawati stared at the pieces. “I worked on that for a week.” “I know. I can see the trunk took ages.” Shalini swallowed. “Can I help you fix it? My brother has proper clay glue. Or I'll help you make a new one at break, for as long as it takes.” Irawati was quiet. Then she took one half. “The glue. And you hold the trunk while it dries.” “Deal.”

qa.q: What did Shalini break?
qa.a: Shalini broke Irawati's clay elephant.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling when she stared at the pieces?
qa.a: Irawati felt upset and disappointed, having worked on the elephant for a week.

qa.q: What made Shalini's apology repairing?
qa.a: She named exactly what she did, took the blame and offered a real fix: glue, or help making a new one.

qa.q: What would change if Shalini had just said “Sorry if you're upset”?
qa.a: Irawati might have felt the apology was empty, and the elephant would have stayed broken.

grounding: Shows a child naming the specific act, saying sorry and offering to help fix what she broke.

passage: I'm Nitin. Last year I borrowed my neighbour Yogesh's comic, the one his uncle brought from Kolkata, and I left it on the bus. I didn't tell him for a week. Every time he asked, I said, “I'll bring it tomorrow.” My stomach hurt every tomorrow. Finally, I went to his door. “I lost your comic on the bus. It's my fault. I should've told you on the first day.” Yogesh's face went red. “My uncle gave me that.” “I know. I asked at the bus depot; it's not there. I've saved my pocket money for a new copy, and Papa says he'll take us to the bookshop on Sunday.” Yogesh was cross for two days. On Sunday, he came.

qa.q: Where did Nitin leave the comic?
qa.a: Nitin left the comic on the bus.

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling during the week of saying “tomorrow”?
qa.a: Nitin felt guilty and anxious, with a stomach ache every time Yogesh asked.

qa.q: What made Nitin's apology more repairing than a vague sorry?
qa.a: Nitin named exactly what happened, admitted the delay, checked the depot and offered a replacement with a plan to buy it.

qa.q: How did Yogesh feel about losing the comic?
qa.a: Yogesh was upset and cross for two days, since his uncle had given it to him, but he came on Sunday.

grounding: Shows a child admitting a specific fault and offering to replace what was lost, which repairs more than a vague sorry.

passage: Class note, Wednesday. Hansa, Class 5. At lunch today a cricket ball went through the staff-room window. By the time I got outside, the boys had scattered, except Tarun. He walked straight up to me, white-faced, and said, “Ma'am, I hit it. It was my shot. I'm sorry.” Not “it was an accident”, not “sorry if anyone's cross”, just what he did. Then he asked, “Can I help clean up the glass, or help fix it?” I didn't let him touch the glass, but I let him hold the tools for the handyman after school. He watched the new pane go in. I've written to his parents that he told the truth first.

qa.q: What did Tarun hold after school?
qa.a: Tarun held the tools for the handyman.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling when he walked up to Hansa?
qa.a: Tarun felt scared and guilty, white-faced, but determined to own up.

qa.q: How did Hansa respond to Tarun's admission, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She kept him away from the glass but let him help the handyman, and told his parents he told the truth first, rewarding honesty.

qa.q: What might the other boys have felt when they scattered?
qa.a: They were probably scared of getting into trouble, unlike Tarun, who stayed and owned up.

grounding: Shows a child admitting a specific fault and offering to help fix it, and an adult rewarding the honesty safely.

passage: The relay was starting in five minutes, and the rain had only just stopped. Bidisha ran up to Jatin at the starting line, breathless. “I'm sorry I told everyone about your nightmare. I shouldn't have.” Jatin's face went hot, remembering the laughing. There was no time for a long talk. “It's okay,” he said quickly. “Let's just run.” They ran, and their team came second. Afterwards, drying off under the tree, Jatin said, “I meant it, I forgive you. But it did hurt. If I tell you something private again, it has to stay private.” Bidisha nodded. “It will. Promise.” Jatin handed her the other half of his towel.

qa.q: Where did the relay team come?
qa.a: Their team came second.

qa.q: What was Jatin feeling when Bidisha apologised at the starting line?
qa.a: Jatin felt embarrassed and hurt remembering the laughing, but rushed to say it was okay because the race was starting.

qa.q: Why was Jatin's later talk under the tree important?
qa.a: It made his forgiveness real while saying clearly that his private things must stay private from now on.

qa.q: How did Bidisha respond to Jatin's boundary?
qa.a: Bidisha nodded and promised to keep private things private.

grounding: Shows a child forgiving a friend quickly under pressure, then making it real while making clear the hurt must not happen again.

passage: For the third Sunday in a row, Madhav and the building boys left Nirmala out of cricket, then came to fetch her when they needed an extra fielder. “Sorry, Nirmala. Come on, let's play.” Every time, she'd said, “It's okay,” and gone, because she hated fights. This Sunday, standing at the top of the stairs, she felt a knot in her chest. It wasn't okay. She walked down slowly. “I'll play. And I forgive you for last week. But if you leave me out again, I'm not coming when you need a fielder.” Madhav blinked, then went red. “Fair. You can bat first.” She did. She hit a four.

qa.q: How many Sundays in a row had Nirmala been left out?
qa.a: Nirmala had been left out for three Sundays in a row.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling at the top of the stairs?
qa.a: Nirmala felt hurt and fed up, with a knot in her chest, realising it wasn't okay.

qa.q: How did Nirmala forgive without accepting the same behaviour again?
qa.a: She agreed to play and forgave last week, but said clearly she wouldn't come if they left her out again.

qa.q: How did Madhav respond to Nirmala's words?
qa.a: Madhav went red, admitted it was fair and let her bat first.

grounding: Shows a child moving from forgiving to avoid conflict to real forgiveness that does not accept the hurtful behaviour again.

passage: “Amandeep? About yesterday.” Pallavi twisted her dupatta. “I'm sorry I called you a copycat in front of everyone. You weren't copying. I was jealous of your project.” Amandeep looked at her for a long moment. “It really hurt.” “I know. I'd be hurt too.” “Why were you jealous?” “Yours had the moving parts. Mine was just a poster.” Amandeep thought. “Okay. I forgive you. For real, not just to stop talking about it.” “Really?” “Really. But next time you're jealous, just say so. Don't call me names.” Pallavi let out a breath. “Deal. Can you show me how the moving parts work?” Amandeep grinned. “Come after school.”

qa.q: What did Pallavi call Amandeep?
qa.a: Pallavi called Amandeep a copycat in front of everyone.

qa.q: What was Pallavi feeling when she called Amandeep a copycat?
qa.a: Pallavi was jealous of Amandeep's project with moving parts.

qa.q: How did Amandeep make the forgiveness real while setting a limit?
qa.a: Amandeep said how much it hurt, forgave for real, and asked Pallavi to name jealousy next time instead of calling names.

qa.q: What does Amandeep's “for real” add to the forgiveness?
qa.a: It shows Amandeep isn't just ending the conflict to avoid it, but genuinely letting the hurt go.

grounding: Shows a child forgiving a friend for real, not just to avoid conflict, while making clear the name-calling must not happen again.

passage: I'm Vikas, and my sister Disha had a tummy ache on Saturday. Mummy asked her where it hurt, and Disha just said, “Everywhere.” Then Mummy got a paper and drew a big circle for a tummy. “Point. And what kind: sharp like a pin, or squeezing, or burning?” Disha pointed low on the right side. “Sharp. Like a pin that stays.” “How bad, one to five?” Disha held up four fingers. I'd never seen her say four about anything; she once fell off her cycle and said two. Mummy's face went serious, and she took Disha to the clinic that afternoon. I don't know what the doctor said, but Mummy said Disha had explained it really well.

qa.q: Where did Disha point on the drawing?
qa.a: Disha pointed low on the right side.

qa.q: What was Disha likely feeling when she held up four fingers?
qa.a: Disha was likely in real pain and worried, since she usually plays pain down.

qa.q: How did Mummy help Disha describe the pain?
qa.a: She drew a tummy for pointing, offered words for the kind of pain and asked for a number, then acted the same afternoon.

qa.q: Why did Vikas notice the number four?
qa.a: Vikas knew Disha usually plays pain down, like saying two after falling off her cycle, so four seemed serious.

grounding: Shows a child describing pain by place, kind and level with a drawing and a scale, and an adult taking it seriously.

passage: Monday: Sarika rubbed her ear at breakfast. When her mother, Sharmila, asked, she said, “It's nothing,” and ran for the bus. The dance show was on Saturday, and she wasn't missing it. Wednesday: At practice she kept tilting her head, and at home she didn't want her favourite crunchy snack. Sharmila noticed. “Show me where it hurts, and how much, one to five.” Sarika pointed inside her left ear. “Three. It throbs when I chew.” “Three since Monday?” Sarika nodded, eyes down. “I didn't want a fuss.” Thursday: The doctor looked in her ear and gave her medicine. By Saturday, she danced.

qa.q: Which ear hurt?
qa.a: Her left ear hurt.

qa.q: Why did Sarika say “It's nothing” on Monday?
qa.a: Sarika was worried a fuss would make her miss the dance show on Saturday, so she hid the pain.

qa.q: What made Sharmila check more closely on Wednesday?
qa.a: She noticed Sarika's changed behaviour, tilting her head and refusing her favourite snack, and asked where and how much it hurt.

qa.q: What was the week like for Sharmila?
qa.a: Sharmila had to watch for clues because Sarika was hiding the pain, and she took her to the doctor once the signs were clear.

grounding: Shows a child downplaying pain to avoid a fuss, and changed behaviour leading an adult to ask about place and level.

passage: Pankaj, you've been rubbing your jaw all day and saying “it's fine”. Let your Hafsa Nani tell you what happened to me. When I was eleven, a back tooth started to ache. I didn't tell anyone; the dentist in our town had a drill that sounded like a tractor. I chewed on the other side. I said “fine” for three weeks. Then one night my cheek swelled up like a mango, and my father carried me to the dentist anyway. He said it was much worse than it would have been. After that, my mother made a rule: say where it hurts, what kind of hurt and how much, even if it's small. So, Pankaj. Where, what kind, how much?

qa.q: What did the dentist's drill sound like to young Hafsa?
qa.a: It sounded like a tractor.

qa.q: Why did young Hafsa keep saying “fine” for three weeks?
qa.a: Young Hafsa was scared of the dentist's loud drill, so she hid the toothache to avoid the fuss.

qa.q: What rule did Hafsa's mother make, and why is it useful?
qa.a: To say where it hurts, what kind of hurt and how much, even if it's small, so problems are noticed early.

qa.q: What was that night like for Hafsa's father?
qa.a: He was probably worried when her cheek swelled and carried her to the dentist straight away.

grounding: Shows a child downplaying pain to avoid the clinic, and learning to describe pain by place, kind and level.

passage: I'm Vishal, Baljeet's neighbour, and I was on their balcony when the wedding argument happened. “I don't want to go,” Baljeet said. His father sighed. “Why not?” Baljeet actually had reasons. “It's four hours. The music is so loud my ears ring. And I don't know anyone my age.” His father didn't say, “Because I said so.” He said, “Fair points. We do have to go; it's your cousin, and Bebe would be hurt. But we can leave after dinner, and you can bring your headphones for the loud part.” Baljeet thought. “And can Vishal come?” They both looked at me. I don't know if Baljeet liked the deal, but he stopped arguing.

qa.q: How long did Baljeet say the wedding lasts?
qa.a: Baljeet said it's four hours.

qa.q: What was Baljeet feeling about going to the wedding?
qa.a: Baljeet felt reluctant and uncomfortable, dreading the loud music and not knowing anyone his age.

qa.q: How did Baljeet's father respect his preference while keeping the limit?
qa.a: He called Baljeet's reasons fair, explained why they had to go, and offered to leave after dinner with headphones.

qa.q: How did Vishal see the argument?
qa.a: Vishal noticed Baljeet had real reasons and that his father listened instead of saying “Because I said so”.

grounding: Shows a child stating a preference with reasons, and a parent explaining the limit respectfully while negotiating.

passage: Monday: “I don't want to do veena any more,” Rukmini told Amma. “I want football on Saturdays.” Amma said, “Tell me why, properly, not just ‘I don't want to.’” Wednesday: Rukmini went to her veena teacher, Joseph Sir, with a list. “One: I've done it for three years and I'm not enjoying it. Two: football is at the same time. Three: I'll still play at home sometimes.” Joseph Sir read it twice. “Those are honest reasons. But the recital is in three weeks, and your group needs you.” Friday: They agreed: Rukmini would play in the recital, then switch to football. She shook Joseph Sir's hand like a grown-up.

qa.q: How many years had Rukmini played the veena?
qa.a: Rukmini had played for three years.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling about veena classes?
qa.a: Rukmini felt tired of veena and no longer enjoyed it, and she was eager to play football instead.

qa.q: How did Rukmini make her preference easier to negotiate?
qa.a: She wrote clear reasons instead of just saying she didn't want to, which led to a fair deal.

qa.q: How did Joseph Sir balance Rukmini's wish with the group's needs?
qa.a: He accepted her reasons as honest but explained the recital needed her, agreeing she could switch afterwards.

grounding: Shows a child stating a preference with reasons over several days, and an adult respecting it while explaining a limit.

passage: Mohit, you told your mother you don't like the new tuition, and she said you're being difficult. Let your Deepika Dadi tell you about my own “I don't like it.” When I was twelve, my father put me in sewing classes after school. Every week I came home and said, “I don't want to go.” He got crosser and crosser. Then my brother told me, “Give him reasons, not just no.” So one evening I said, “Babuji, I get headaches from the tiny stitches, the class is at the same time as the science club, and science is what I love.” He was quiet for a long time. Then he said, “Try science for one term.” I became a science teacher, Mohit. Give reasons.

qa.q: What class did young Deepika's father put her in?
qa.a: He put her in sewing classes after school.

qa.q: What was young Deepika feeling every week when she came home?
qa.a: She felt unhappy and frustrated with the sewing class, missing the science she loved.

qa.q: What choice did Deepika make that changed her father's mind?
qa.a: She followed her brother's advice and gave clear reasons: the headaches, the clash with science club and her love of science.

qa.q: How did her father respond once he heard reasons?
qa.a: He was quiet for a long time, then agreed she could try science for one term.

grounding: Shows a child stating a preference and learning to give reasons, which helps an adult listen and negotiate.

passage: At the village school's kabaddi practice, Leela stopped the game for the fourth time. “Masterji! Chinmay's foot went over the line again! That's cheating!” Chinmay rolled his eyes. The others groaned. Masterji walked over. “Was it over?” he asked Chinmay. Chinmay looked. “A little. Sorry.” Masterji turned to Leela. “You were right about the line. You care about fairness, and that's good.” Leela beamed. “But four stops in ten minutes, and shouting ‘cheating’, make people stop listening. Next time, tell Chinmay calmly first: ‘Your foot's over.’ Come to me if it keeps happening, or if someone could get hurt.” Leela thought about it and nodded.

qa.q: How many times had Leela stopped the game?
qa.a: Leela had stopped the game four times.

qa.q: What was Leela feeling when she shouted “That's cheating”?
qa.a: Leela felt indignant and frustrated about the unfair foot over the line.

qa.q: What guidance did Masterji give Leela about tone?
qa.a: To tell Chinmay calmly first, and come to him if it keeps happening or someone could get hurt.

qa.q: How did the other players react to the stops?
qa.a: They groaned, tired of the game being stopped and of the shouting.

grounding: Shows a child's genuine fairness complaint sliding into constant reporting, and an adult guiding her on tone.

passage: At the football club in São Paulo, Kaito was captain again, and again he picked his three best friends first. Rafael, left until nearly last, marched to the coach. “It's not fair! Kaito always picks his friends. He's a cheat and a bully!” The coach raised a hand. “Hold on. Is he breaking a rule?” Rafael paused. “No. But it's unfair.” “That's a real point, and I'm glad you told me. ‘Cheat’ and ‘bully’ aren't true, though, and they make people stop listening.” Rafael's face went red. “So what do I say?” “Say, ‘Can we rotate captains, so everyone gets picked early sometimes?’” Rafael said it at the team meeting. From then on, captains rotated weekly.

qa.q: How often did captains rotate after the meeting?
qa.a: Captains rotated weekly.

qa.q: What was Rafael feeling as he marched to the coach?
qa.a: Rafael felt angry and hurt at being picked nearly last again, and it seemed unfair.

qa.q: How did the coach help Rafael turn his complaint into something useful?
qa.a: He agreed the fairness point was real but asked Rafael to drop the untrue labels and suggest a rotation instead.

qa.q: What would change if Rafael had called Kaito a cheat at the team meeting?
qa.a: Kaito and his friends would probably get defensive, and the fair idea of rotating captains might have been ignored.

grounding: Shows a child's genuine fairness criticism turning into name-calling, and an adult guiding the tone into a fair proposal.

passage: Every evening at the hostel, Kalyani came to Nirmala Ma'am's office with a list. “Rupa jumped the bathroom queue. Asha had her light on after ten. Someone took two chapatis.” Nirmala Ma'am listened, then patted the chair. “Kalyani, you notice when things are unfair, and that matters. Some of these are small, though. What could you do about the queue yourself?” Kalyani frowned. “Tell Rupa?” “Yes, calmly. If someone's being hurt, or it's unsafe, or talking doesn't work, then you come to me. Always.” The next evening there was only one thing on the list: “The fire exit is blocked by trunks.” Nirmala Ma'am got up at once.

qa.q: What was blocking the fire exit?
qa.a: Trunks were blocking the fire exit.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling as she brought her list each evening?
qa.a: Kalyani felt strongly that the small rule-breaks were unfair and wanted them fixed.

qa.q: What guidance did Nirmala Ma'am give Kalyani?
qa.a: To handle small things calmly with the person first, and to come to her whenever someone is hurt, something is unsafe or talking doesn't work.

qa.q: How did Nirmala Ma'am respond to the blocked fire exit?
qa.a: She got up at once, showing that serious safety reports are exactly what she wants to hear.

grounding: Shows a child's genuine concern for fairness sliding into tale-telling, and an adult guiding when to speak to peers and when to report.
